title: More Is Not More: What Matters for Opinion Diversity in LLM Simulations?
claim: Intervention gains are confounded when dimensions are upgraded together; a factorial grid separates input conditioning from interaction architecture.
layout: Single grid, depth rows by architecture columns, diagonal arrow, low-cost tricks beneath
description: A large 5×3 grid is the main element. Rows are persona depth levels, from None at the bottom to Pro at the top. Each row has a blue-outlined text box with an example prompt, such as "You are a helpful assistant" or a long Sarah Johnson backstory. A blue vertical gradient bar on the left is labeled Input Conditioning, from less to more detail. The columns are interaction architectures, with a gradient bar across the top running from lower to higher complexity. Each column has an icon header: Single-Call in gray, Multi-Turn Self-Prompting in orange with numbered speech bubbles, and Multi-Agent Discussion in green with a circle of people. A red dashed diagonal arrow labeled "Typical product upgrade path" runs from a starred Baseline in the bottom-left cell to the top-right cell. A bracket on the right notes that the same 20 individuals are used at every level. Below the grid, four dashed orange boxes list the low-cost tricks, branching from the baseline.
caption: Factorial experimental design. The vertical axis varies input conditioning through five levels of persona depth (None, Role, Basic, Mid, Pro). The horizontal axis varies interaction architecture across three conditions: Single-Call, Multi-Turn Self-Prompting, and Multi-Agent Discussion. The dashed diagonal indicates the typical co-evolution observed in practice, where both dimensions are upgraded simultaneously. Four low-cost tricks (bottom) are evaluated at the Single-Call $\times$ None baseline.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate diverse human opinions in open-ended tasks such as synthetic surveys, focus group modeling, and public opinion prediction. However, LLM outputs exhibit systematic opinion homogenization, and a simulation cannot reproduce a population's opinion distribution without first covering its range of viewpoints. Interventions to increase diversity are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics and are typically deployed and upgraded simultaneously, making it difficult to attribute gains to specific components. We design a factorial experiment that separates two primary intervention dimensions: input conditioning (operationalized through persona depth) and interaction architecture. We evaluate all conditions on 100 real-user open-ended questions across 7 models, measuring diversity with multiple complementary metrics. Our findings challenge several common assumptions. First, more persona detail does not monotonically increase diversity. The initial step of persona conditioning already captures the majority of the gain, while further elaboration with demographic detail does not consistently improve and can reduce diversity on some models; a blinded human evaluation of matched Role and Basic responses points in the same direction. Second, rather than seeking a single best interaction architecture, we find that different architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions. Combining multiple architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any one. Third, commonly attempted low-cost alternatives such as raising sampling temperature and adding diversity instructions produce negligible effects compared to structured interventions. Overall, our results indicate that, within the tested settings, diversity does not scale along any single dimension but is sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions.
